opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to start by saying that it isn't one community with one view. People tend to talk about "the x-risk crowd" as if it's a monolith, but there's a real spectrum.

At one end, some people believe catastrophic outcomes from very capable systems are likely enough, and close enough, that they should dominate how we prioritize research and policy. At the other end, many researchers think the risk is speculative and that the framing pulls attention away from harms happening right now: bias, misinformation, concentration of power, systems failing in ways that hit the people least able to absorb it. And a lot of people sit in the middle. They take long-term risk seriously but want it grounded in empirical work we can actually measure today.

My own view is that some of the most useful work comes from that middle ground. I care a lot about rigor. When a claim is about some hypothetical future system with abilities we can't yet observe, it's very hard to falsify, and it's hard to design interventions you know are working. That doesn't make the concern illegitimate. But I'd like more of the energy channeled into things we can study: how models behave out of distribution, how robust safety training is, what actually happens when you compress or fine-tune a model, and where evaluations break down.

I also worry about what the framing does to policy. If the conversation fixates on a single dramatic scenario, it can justify concentrating control of the technology in a few hands, often in the name of safety. That carries its own risks. It shuts out researchers in parts of the world who are already under-resourced, and it reduces the diversity of people looking at these systems critically.

So I welcome the range of views, and I think the disagreement is healthy. The thing I push for is humility on all sides. We're quite bad at predicting how capabilities emerge. Scale hasn't always delivered what people expected, and smaller, more efficient models keep surprising us. Given that uncertainty, I'd rather we invest in measurement, openness, and broad participation, which help whether you're worried about next year's harms or harms decades out.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a much more heterogeneous community than it gets credit for, and I say that as someone who's often cast as a skeptic. When people say "the existential-risk community," they tend to picture one thing, which is a very specific set of assumptions: that scaling continues indefinitely, that you get discontinuous capability jumps, and that you end up with a system whose goals are misaligned in a way we can't detect or correct. And there is a group of people who hold that view quite strongly. But if you actually sit down with researchers who work on this, you find a pretty wide spread.

At one end, you have folks who are genuinely focused on the long-horizon, speculative scenarios, where the methodology is largely philosophical or decision-theoretic. A lot of that work is thought experiments and probability estimates, and it's not easy to falsify. I have real reservations about how much weight that should carry in policy conversations, because it can crowd out empirical questions.

Then you have a middle group that I find much more interesting, who are using the language of catastrophic risk but whose actual day-to-day work looks like good machine learning research: interpretability, evaluations, red-teaming, understanding what emergent behavior actually is and whether it's an artifact of how we measure things. I'd put myself closer to that camp in terms of what I think is tractable, even if I'd frame the motivation differently. A lot of my own work on how models fail, who they fail for, how compression and training choices shape behavior, is about the same underlying question: do we actually understand what these systems are doing?

And then at the other end you have people who are quite practical about governance, compute thresholds, reporting, incident tracking. Some of that is useful. Some of it, I'd argue, is built on proxies that don't hold up, like treating training FLOPs as a reliable signal of risk when the relationship between compute and capability has been changing fast.

So my view is: the disagreement I have isn't really with the existence of the field. It's with how much certainty gets attached to the speculative end, and how often that certainty pulls attention and resources away from the harms that are already measurable today, around language coverage, around who gets left out of these systems, around safety evaluations that mostly work for English. Those aren't competing concerns in principle, but in practice they compete for the same researchers and the same policy bandwidth. I'd like to see the empirical wing of that community get more of the airtime.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very broad community, and it’s useful to distinguish the different questions people are asking. Some work focuses on whether we can understand and control increasingly capable systems. Some focuses on misuse, and some on scenarios where systems act in ways that are fundamentally at odds with human interests. Those involve different assumptions and different kinds of evidence.

For me, the important question is how you make progress on those concerns in a way that can be tested. Can you articulate the assumptions behind a risk, identify what evidence would change your mind, and connect it to a concrete research problem?

I also don’t think addressing risks we can observe today and thinking about longer-term risks have to be competing priorities. Work on understanding model behavior, evaluating failures, and improving accountability can be valuable across both. But we should be clear about where we have evidence and where we’re extrapolating.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very broad community, and it’s useful to distinguish the approaches rather than treat it as one school of thought. Some people focus on theoretical questions about aligning a much more capable future system. Others work empirically on systems we have today—trying to understand their behavior, evaluate their limitations, and make them more reliable.

Where I tend to put my emphasis is on making the assumptions explicit. What capability are we concerned about? What would have to happen for that capability to lead to harm? And what evidence would change our assessment? We need room to investigate uncertain risks, but we also need ways to test whether the work is actually making progress. And I don’t think concern about future systems should displace work on the harms people are experiencing today.
